query: Earlier empirical-potential and first-principles studies primarily targeted phase-transition temperature, while other fusion properties remain difficult because they require free energies on both sides of the transition with vibrational entropy, anharmonicity, and electron–vibration coupling retained. Explicit ab initio free-energy evaluation is highly accurate but depends on costly molecular dynamics. TOR-TILD increased throughput for elemental and binary systems, yet slows substantially for multicomponent high-entropy systems. Under the constraint that the free energies of both solid and fluid states and the relevant entropy terms remain faithful, what single testable methodological hypothesis could substantially reduce the cost of obtaining fusion and high-temperature thermodynamic properties? State the proposed intervention and why it should work, predict its speed and fidelity relative to explicit ab initio molecular-dynamics workflows and TOR-TILD, define composition and temperature boundaries, cite supporting evidence from prior elemental or binary results, and specify a decisive benchmark of phase free energies and derived observables that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: An active‐learning framework that couples a deep-learning interatomic potential with on‐the‐fly, sparse DFT-based free energy corrections via uncertainty-aware umbrella integration (using Gaussian process regression) can faithfully reproduce the fusion free energy curves—including full vibrational anharmonicity and electron–vibration coupling—in both the solid and fluid phases of multicomponent high‐entropy systems at a computational cost an order of magnitude lower than explicit AIMD or TOR-TILD methods.
generation.material_initial_state: A multicomponent high‐entropy alloy (e.g., MoNbTaW) prepared in its equilibrium solid state near melting temperature.
generation.intervention: Develop and deploy an active-learning ML potential (e.g., deep potential model) that rapidly generates MD trajectories across the solid–fluid transition; intermittently select representative configurations for high-fidelity DFT evaluations that capture anharmonic effects and electron–vibration coupling, and integrate these corrections via umbrella integration with Gaussian process regression.
generation.conditions: Simulation across the fusion temperature range (approximately 0.9Tm to 1.1Tm) for systems with increasing compositional complexity (moving from elemental/binary to multicomponent/HEA systems) where free energies must include accurate vibrational and electronic entropy contributions.
generation.structural_mediator: The accuracy of the free energy curve is mediated by capturing the covariance of atomic displacements (vibrational entropy) and subtle electron–vibration interactions in both phases, which are directly corrected by the DFT reweighting step.
generation.mechanism: The ML potential efficiently samples the phase space, while active learning identifies key configurations where anharmonic and electron–vibration effects are prominent. Sparse but strategically obtained DFT corrections are then seamlessly integrated using umbrella integration with GPR to yield a corrected free energy profile. This synergy reduces the expensive MD time and drastically lowers the number of ab initio evaluations required while retaining high fidelity in the computed thermodynamic properties.
generation.predicted_outcome: The method will produce fusion free energy curves and derived high-temperature thermodynamic observables (e.g., vibrational entropy, latent heat) that agree within experimental and AIMD error bars yet reduce the computational cost by roughly an order of magnitude relative to explicit AIMD or TOR-TILD workflows.
generation.baseline: Explicit ab initio MD simulations (as in PMC9141984 studies) and TOR-TILD free energy integration methods tested for elemental and binary systems (e.g., FCC Al, BCC Na).
generation.boundary: The approach is expected to be effective for systems where the cost of sampling can be substantially reduced via active learning; however, if electron–vibration coupling or anharmonic effects are so complex that sparse DFT corrections fail to capture them, the method may break down. Also, its efficacy may be limited in systems with extreme anharmonicity or where the active-learning convergence stalls.
generation.uncertainty: This proposal extends the success of ML potential accelerated free energy sampling (as seen in PMC10569033 and PMC5419702) to complex high-entropy systems, while combining them with uncertainty-quantified umbrella integration. New in this proposal is the on-the-fly active learning for rigorous free energy correction especially targeting electron–vibration coupling in multicomponent systems. Uncertainty remains regarding how many DFT corrections are needed and whether they can fully capture the intricate coupling effects in HEAs (see PMC9141984::web::026::4_conclusions for cautions on anharmonicity limits).

falsification_experiment.design: Apply the integrated active-learning ML potential method to a well-characterized multicomponent high-entropy alloy (e.g., MoNbTaW) near its melting point. Run MD simulations across the fusion transition using the ML potential, interspersed with DFT evaluations selected by the active-learning module. Compute the solid and fluid free energy curves via umbrella integration with GPR and compare these curves—and derived thermodynamic properties such as latent heat and vibrational entropy—to those obtained from full explicit AIMD and TOR-TILD simulations.
measurements: Free energy differences and curves across the solid–fluid transition
Derived observables such as vibrational entropy, latent heat, and phase-transition temperature
Computational cost (wall-clock time and number of DFT evaluations)
Uncertainty quantification via Gaussian process regression confidence intervals
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the ML-based method fails to reproduce the AIMD/TOR-TILD free energy curves within acceptable experimental and simulation error margins, or if it does not achieve at least a tenfold reduction in computational cost, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Predicting the rate constants of elementary reaction steps is key for the computational modeling of catalytic processes. Within transition state theory (TST), this requires an accurate estimation of the corresponding free energy barriers. While sophisticated methods for estimating free energy differences exist, these typically require extensive (biased) molecular dynamics simulations that are computationally prohibitive with the first-principles electronic structure methods that are typically used in catalysis research. In this contribution, we show that machine-learning (ML) interatomic potentials can be trained in an automated iterative workflow to perform such free energy calculations at a much reduced computational cost as compared to a direct density functional theory (DFT) based evaluation. For the decomposition of CHO on Rh(111), we find that thermal effects are substantial and lead to a decrease in the free energy barrier, which can be vanishingly small, depending on the DFT functional used. We perform phonon calculations as implemented in phonopy [] to obtain force constants and vibrational frequencies, and then calculate vibrational entropy as discussed in Section 2.3. Rather than calculating the thermal expansion ab initio, as in the traditional quasiharmonic approximation [], we simply evaluate the force constants at the experimentally known temperature-dependent lattice constant a(T). Electronic entropy is evaluated as with D(E) the electronic density of states calculated from a structure with lattice constant a(T), and fT,μ the Fermi-Dirac occupation function. The chemical potential μ is obtained as a function of T using the program Felect [].

The method applies generally to solids, but the particular implementation given here relies on the accuracy of a Gaussian approximation to the distribution function. Hence it is most likely to work when the atomic displacements are small, and it is likely to fail in molecular solids where coherent bond rotations are present. Although we mainly demonstrated the method for elemental solids, it also holds in principle for complex crystalline and noncrystalline solids. We give an example of such an application for the MoNbTaW high entropy alloy. The quasiharmonic method may be equally accurate and more efficient than our AIMD method when anharmonicity mainly enters through thermal expansion, but a simulation-based approach in principle includes additional anharmonic contributions. Doing so may require correlations beyond those captured by the Gaussian approximation (see Section 3.3.1). Our simulation-based approach seems most useful when the simulation has already been completed for other purposes. Then, the entropy comes essentially for free on top of whatever other information was sought.
